I'll write about the strange, quiet magic of ordinary moments.

---

There's a particular silence that happens when snow is falling. Not the absence of sound, but a *softening* of it—cars become distant hums, voices muffle, and the world seems to hold its breath. I was walking home once during a storm like this, and a single snowflake landed on my eyelash. I stopped walking. Just stood there in the middle of the sidewalk, feeling the cold weight of it, watching it melt into a tiny drop against my skin. I was late for something, I'm sure. I don't remember what. I remember the snowflake.

People talk about peak experiences—mountaintops, concerts, falling in love. But I think the best moments are smaller. The way light comes through a kitchen window at 4pm in winter, turning dust motes into something almost holy. The specific sound of a friend laughing at something you said three minutes ago, when you've already forgotten the joke. Finding a book you loved as a child, opening it randomly, and smelling the pages—that particular vanilla-and-paper scent that somehow transports you instantly, completely, back to being eight years old and believing anything was possible.

I think we're all just walking around, half-remembering versions of ourselves. The person I was at twenty would barely recognize me now. The person I'll be at sixty probably won't either. And yet here I am, continuous somehow, carrying all of it. It's strange. It's sad, sometimes. But also—what a gift, to keep becoming someone new while somehow remaining yourself.

Anyway. That's what I was thinking about today. The snowflake. The light. The book you find in a box in your parents' basement.

What are you thinking about?
